title: AI Agents and Non-Human Identities: The Security Risks and How to Reduce Them
content_md: TL;DR AI agents are non-human identities: They decide which systems to call, then authenticate with API keys, OAuth tokens, and service accounts. The risk sits in the credentials: Agents get broad, standing permissions, their secrets spread into prompts, logs, tickets, code, and MCP configuration files, and many keys outlive the person who created them. Attackers log in rather than break in: Whoever holds a leaked agent credential logs in as the agent and inherits whatever it can reach. Start with inventory and ownership: List every agent and its credentials, inside and outside the vault, and give each one a named owner. Then shrink and guard access: Scope permissions to the task, prefer short-lived credentials, keep secrets out of prompts and shared tools, and monitor agent activity with a revocation plan. AI agents are non-human identities (NHIs) that make their own decisions and can take direct actions that affect the world around them. They choose which systems to call and then authenticate with API keys, OAuth tokens, and service accounts. The credentials they hold to your critical systems are the most direct path an attacker has into your data. This guide is for security, application security, and platform teams rolling out AI agents. It explains why agents need to be treated like any other non-human identity, seven risks they introduce, and six controls that reduce those concerns.
